title: Mars: The Red Planet's Biggest Secrets

lines: On Mars, there is a volcano so wide it would cover the state of Arizona.
There is a canyon long enough to stretch across the entire United States.
There is snow made of frozen carbon dioxide, and sunsets that glow blue.
And there is a moon that rises in the west, crosses the sky in a few hours, and is slowly falling toward the planet.
Mars is our neighbour, the most explored planet after Earth, and still one of the strangest worlds we know.
So today, let's take a proper tour of the red planet.

scenes.callout: Mars is about half Earth's width
lines: Mars is about half as wide as Earth.
Its diameter is roughly six thousand eight hundred kilometres, and it has only about one tenth of Earth's mass.
That means the gravity is weak. On Mars you would weigh only about thirty eight percent of what you weigh here.
Mars orbits about two hundred and twenty eight million kilometres from the Sun, around one and a half times farther than Earth.
One trip around the Sun takes six hundred and eighty seven Earth days, so a Martian year is almost two of ours.
But a day on Mars feels surprisingly familiar.
A Martian day, called a sol, lasts about twenty four and a half hours, only around forty minutes longer than ours.
Mars is also tilted about twenty five degrees, very close to Earth's tilt, so it has seasons too.
And the famous red colour? That is rust. Iron in the dust and rocks has oxidised, painting the whole planet red.
Mars is home to the biggest volcano in the solar system: Olympus Mons.
It is about six hundred kilometres across, roughly the size of Arizona.
Depending on where you measure from, it rises about twenty two to twenty six kilometres high.
That is around two and a half to three times the height of Mount Everest.
Yet its slopes are so gentle, only about five percent on average, that if you stood on it, you might not even realise you were on a mountain.
At the top sits a crater made of six overlapping collapse pits, together about eighty five kilometres wide.
So why is it so huge?
On Earth, hotspots like the one under Hawaii stay put while the plate above them slides along, so the lava builds a chain of islands instead of one giant mountain.
Mars has very little plate movement, so its volcanoes sat over the same hotspot and just kept growing.
Lower gravity helped too, letting lava pile up higher before the mountain sank under its own weight.
Olympus Mons has about one hundred times the volume of Mauna Loa, Earth's largest volcano.
Just east of those volcanoes, a giant scar cuts across the face of Mars.
It is called Valles Marineris, and it is the largest canyon system in the solar system.
It is about four thousand kilometres long. On Earth, it would stretch from Los Angeles all the way to the Atlantic coast.
It is about two hundred kilometres wide and up to about seven kilometres deep.
That makes it roughly ten times longer, twenty times wider and five times deeper than the Grand Canyon.

Unlike the Grand Canyon, it was not carved mainly by a river. Scientists think it started as the crust cracked and pulled apart along faults, around three and a half billion years ago, as the volcanic region next door swelled up.

scenes.callout: Air pressure: less than 1% of Earth's
lines: If you stepped outside on Mars, you would need a spacesuit right away.
The air is about ninety five percent carbon dioxide, with very little oxygen.
And it is incredibly thin. The pressure at the surface is less than one percent of Earth's.
It is also cold. The average temperature is around minus sixty degrees Celsius.
On a summer afternoon near the equator, the ground can reach about twenty degrees, but at night it can drop to around minus one hundred and fifty.
And then there is the dust.
Every few Earth years, dust storms can grow until they wrap around the entire planet.
In twenty eighteen, a storm spotted at the end of May covered all of Mars within about three weeks.
It blocked the sunlight that NASA's Opportunity rover needed for power.
Opportunity sent its last message in June twenty eighteen, and after eight months of trying to wake it up, NASA ended the mission.
Mars also has dust devils, spinning whirlwinds that form when the ground is warmer than the air above it.
In twenty twenty three, the Perseverance rover filmed one about sixty metres wide, and scientists estimated from its shadow that it may have been around two kilometres tall.
But the most beautiful Martian weather might be the sunset.
In twenty fifteen, the Curiosity rover filmed the Sun going down, and the sky around it glowed blue.
On Earth, sunsets turn red and orange. On Mars, the fine dust lets blue light pass through more easily near the Sun, so the colours are flipped.
Mars even has snow, and some of it is not made of water.
In twenty twelve, NASA announced that its Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter had detected carbon dioxide snow falling over the south pole.
NASA called it the only known example of carbon dioxide snow falling anywhere in our solar system.
Every winter, a layer of dry ice frosts over the poles, then turns back into gas in spring, on top of permanent caps that contain water ice.
Mars has two small moons, and their names are a little scary.
In August eighteen seventy seven, astronomer Asaph Hall discovered both of them, Deimos first and then Phobos six nights later.
They are named after the sons of Ares, the Greek god of war. Phobos means fear, and Deimos means dread.
They are tiny and lumpy, more like potatoes than round moons. Phobos is only about twenty two kilometres across, and Deimos about twelve.

scenes.callout: Phobos orbits Mars about 3 times a day
lines: Phobos orbits just six thousand kilometres above the surface, closer to its planet than any other known moon.
It whips around Mars about three times a day, faster than Mars itself spins.
So from the ground, Phobos rises in the west and sets in the east.
And it is doomed. Phobos is spiralling inward by about one point eight metres every century.
Within tens of millions of years, NASA estimates about fifty million, it will either crash into Mars or be torn apart into a ring.
Today, Mars is a frozen desert. But it was not always this way.
Billions of years ago, Mars was probably warmer and wetter, and it once had a global magnetic field.
NASA's Curiosity rover, exploring Gale Crater since twenty twelve, found that the crater once held lakes and streams around three and a half billion years ago.
Those lakes may have dried out and refilled again and again, and scientists say they could have supported life, if any existed.
The Perseverance rover landed in Jezero Crater, an ancient lake bed with a dried river delta.
Its ground penetrating radar looked about twenty metres underground and found layers of lake sediment.
Water has not disappeared completely either. Mars still holds a lot of ice in its polar caps, and NASA maps show likely ice within a metre of the surface in parts of the northern half of the planet.
Our up-close story with Mars began in July nineteen sixty five, when NASA's Mariner four flew past.
It sent back twenty one full images, the first close-up pictures of another planet, showing a cratered, Moon-like surface.
In nineteen seventy one, the Soviet Mars three lander made the first soft landing, but it stopped transmitting after less than twenty seconds.
Then on July twentieth, nineteen seventy six, NASA's Viking one landed safely, and its very first picture showed its own footpad on the Martian ground.
The first rover, Sojourner, arrived on July fourth, nineteen ninety seven. It was about the size of a microwave oven.
In twenty oh four, the twin rovers Spirit and Opportunity landed. Each was planned to work for about ninety days.
Spirit kept going until twenty ten. Opportunity lasted almost fifteen years and drove more than forty five kilometres.
Curiosity, the size of a car, landed in August twenty twelve, and Perseverance followed in February twenty twenty one.
Perseverance brought a passenger: a tiny helicopter called Ingenuity.
On April nineteenth, twenty twenty one, it made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet.
It was designed for at most five test flights. It ended up flying seventy two times, covering about seventeen kilometres, before its mission ended in January twenty twenty four.
Meanwhile, Perseverance has been sealing rock samples in tubes. NASA's original plan to bring them home was cancelled in twenty twenty six, so for now, those samples are waiting on Mars.
So could humans ever go?
Getting there is a matter of timing. Earth and Mars line up for a good launch window only about every twenty six months.
Even then, the trip takes about six to nine months. Perseverance made it in about seven.
Once you arrive, a message home takes between about three and twenty two minutes each way, depending on where the planets are.

Radiation is a big danger, because Mars has no global magnetic field and only a thin atmosphere to shield you. But there is hope. An experiment on Perseverance called MOXIE made oxygen out of the Martian air, about one hundred and twenty two grams in total.
And that buried ice could one day give astronauts water to drink and even fuel for the trip home.
Mars is cold, dusty and dangerous, but it is also the planet most like our own.
It has giant volcanoes, a canyon as long as a continent, blue sunsets and a moon that is falling out of the sky.
Maybe one day, someone watching this will be the first to stand there.
Would you go? Tell me in the comments, and subscribe for more trips across the solar system.

description:
Mars has a volcano the size of Arizona, a canyon as long as the United States, blue sunsets, carbon-dioxide snow, and a moon that is slowly falling toward it. In this video we tour the red planet: Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris, global dust storms, Phobos and Deimos, the evidence for ancient lakes, every milestone from Mariner 4 to Ingenuity, and what it would take for humans to live there.

All visuals are original computer-generated renders (not real photographs). Narration is AI-generated.
